title: “WHAT ABOUT HIM?”
paragraphs: “WHAT ABOUT HIM?”
Peter had just heard the prophecy of his own death.

Not a gentle death.
Not retirement in peace.

But a road that would stretch his arms and cost him everything.
Jesus had just told him: “You will stretch out your hands…” (John 21:18).
And Peter felt it.

The weight.
The future.
The cross-shaped destiny.
So he did what many of us do when obedience starts to feel heavy.
He looked sideways.
John was walking nearby—the disciple Jesus loved, calm, quiet, close to the Master.
Peter pointed.
“Lord… what about him?” (John 21:21)
Not a theological question.
A comparison question.

Why is my road hard?
Why does his look easier?
Why my suffering?
Why his closeness?
And Jesus gave one of the sharpest, most liberating answers in the entire Gospel.

“If I want him to remain until I return, what is that to you?
You… follow Me.” (John 21:22)
Translation?

Peter.
Eyes forward.
Comparison is a thief of obedience.
When you stare at someone else’s calling, you start doubting your own.
When you measure your suffering against someone else’s blessing, bitterness grows.
But Jesus shuts the door on comparison.

Not harshly.
Lovingly.
Because the Kingdom of God does not run on competition.
It runs on calling.

John had his story.
Peter had his.

John would write the Gospel.
Peter would shepherd the church.
Both would suffer.
Both would glorify Christ.

Different roads.
Same Savior.
And here’s the deeper grace hiding in the moment.
The man asking the question—Peter—was the same man who once denied Jesus three times.
Failure was his past.
But Jesus had already restored him three times:

“Feed My lambs.”
“Tend My sheep.”
“Feed My sheep.” (John 21:15–17)
The Gospel always moves like this:
Failure → Restoration → Calling.
Not because Peter was strong.
But because Jesus saves sinners and reassigns their future.
Your story might not look like someone else’s.

Your road may feel heavier.
Your timing slower.
Your calling quieter.
But Jesus’ words still echo through every generation:
“What is that to you?”

Not your comparison.
Not your scoreboard.
Not your timeline.
Just this:
Follow Me.
And the beautiful scandal of grace?
The One who calls you to follow already walked the road of suffering first.
He carried the cross.
He died for our sin.
He rose again so that broken disciples—like Peter… like us—could live forgiven and sent.
So today, lift your eyes.
Not sideways.
Upward.
The King is still calling.
Follow Him.
We tell the stories that shame tried to erase.
